draft.title: Hess's law
card: Hess's law says the enthalpy change (ΔH) of a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or in several. It depends only on the starting reactants and the final products.
So we can add equations to get a target equation, and add their ΔH values to get its ΔH. Substances that appear on both sides cancel out.
If an equation is reversed, change the sign of its ΔH. If it is multiplied by a number, multiply its ΔH by the same number.
This lets us find ΔH for a reaction that is hard to measure directly, using reactions whose ΔH values are known.
draft.remember: Add the equations and add the ΔH values. Reverse flips the sign, multiplying scales it.

a.q: Reaction 1 has ΔH = -100 kJ. Reaction 2 has ΔH = -50 kJ. Adding the two equations gives the target reaction. What is its ΔH?
a.why: By Hess's law, the ΔH values of added equations are added: -100 + -50 = -150 kJ. Taking the difference (-50 kJ) is tempting, but nothing is reversed here, so the values are simply summed.
a.clue: Adding equations means adding their ΔH values.

b.q: A → B has ΔH = +40 kJ. Mia needs the ΔH for B → A. She also needs the ΔH for 2A → 2B. Which pair is correct?
opts: B → A is -40 kJ, and 2A → 2B is +80 kJ
B → A is +40 kJ, and 2A → 2B is +80 kJ
B → A is -40 kJ, and 2A → 2B is +40 kJ
B → A is -80 kJ, and 2A → 2B is -40 kJ
b.why: Reversing A → B flips the sign, so B → A is -40 kJ. Doubling the equation doubles ΔH, so 2A → 2B is +80 kJ. Keeping +40 kJ for the doubled equation ignores that twice as much reacts.
b.clue: One change flips the sign. The other changes the size.

b.best: B → A is -40 kJ, and 2A → 2B is +80 kJ
